newsitem.title: USA: Philip Morris CEO to be questioned on Thursday.
newsitem.headline: Philip Morris CEO to be questioned on Thursday.

text.p: Philip Morris Cos. Inc. Chief Executive Geoffrey Bible will be questioned on Thursday as part of Florida's multibillion-dollar lawsuit against the tobacco industry, a court official ruled Tuesday.

William Rutter, a former judge who has been assigned the task of handling motions regarding the introduction of evidence and testimony from witnesses in the case, said Bible would be questioned in a pretrial hearing at 8 a.m. EDT on Thursday in Rutter's office.

The state of Florida has sued 13 cigarette makers to recover the costs of treating Medicaid recipients for smoking-related illnesses. The state has also alleged the tobacco industry was guilty of racketeering and fraud and is seeking $12.3 billion in compensatory and punitive damages.
Rutter agreed Tuesday to moderate the three-hour videotaped questioning at the request of the tobacco companies' attorneys.

Attorney Steve Lockman, representing Philip Morris, said Rutter's presence was needed to prevent the "ugly ... and humiliating" way James Morgan, CEO of Philip Morris Inc., the company's subsidiary, was treated during his five-hour deposition in New York last month.
In one exchange between Morgan and one of the attorneys representing Florida, the attorney characterized Morgan as a "salesman."

When Morgan denied any knowledge of how a cigarette is made, the attorney said: "As far as this company is concerned, you have already disavowed any knowledge of production of the cigarette, you have disavowed any knowledge of the science of the cigarette ... so it would seem that your singular function in this company is to sell the product that the company produces. Am I wrong in this regard?"

Bible will be the first of two top cigarette executives to be questioned this week in West Palm Beach, Fla. Steven Goldstone, chairman and chief executive officer of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp., the parent company of R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., will undergo state questioning on Friday.

W.C. Gentry, one of Florida's attorneys, said that he supported the way Morgan had been questioned. "I see nothing wrong in putting hard questions to witnesses who are acting evasive," he said. Florida lawyers did not object to Rutter acting as moderator.
Gentry said the state still planned on asking tough questions. "We are sick and tired of having (tobacco) witnesses well prepared in advance. We want responsive answers," he said.

Florida's lawsuit is the first of 40 filed by state attorneys general against the industry to go to trial. Jury selection was expected to take the rest of the month, with opening statements taking place soon after Labor Day.
To date, 172 of the 336 potential jurors initially summoned for the trial have been dismissed for health or financial reasons or personal prejudices.
